Introduction

Starting a Nursing Facility in Georgia represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals needing 24-hour skilled nursing, rehabilitation, and personal care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), through its Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD). Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through the Georgia Medicaid State Plan and associated waivers, often managed by Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) like Peach State, Amerigroup, WellCare, and CareSource.

With significant demand, evidenced by over 7,000 individuals on Medicaid waiver waiting lists, and robust Medicaid per diem rates ranging from $589.62 to $707.54 per day, Georgia offers a market with strong financial opportunity for providers prepared to navigate its rigorous licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s commitment to enhancing its reimbursement budget underscores the viability for new and existing operators who can deliver high-quality care, particularly in specialized areas like memory care and post-acute rehabilitation.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Nursing Facility in Georgia, from understanding state and federal regulations and securing your license to staffing your facility, managing reimbursement, and preparing for inspections. Whether you are acquiring an existing facility or building from the ground up, this framework will help you establish a foundation for long-term success.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Georgia’s Nursing Facility Regulations

  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Georgia’s Nursing Facility Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in opening a nursing facility. Georgia regulates Nursing Facilities through the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD), which is responsible for the initial licensure, ongoing monitoring, and complaint investigations for all nursing homes in the state. The primary state-level rules are outlined in DCH Chapter 111-8-25. Because most nursing facilities serve residents covered by Medicare or Medicaid, providers must also comply with stringent federal frameworks, most notably the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) regulations found in 42 CFR Part 483.

The regulatory framework in Georgia emphasizes a resident-centered approach, with a strong focus on resident rights, safety, quality of care, clinical services, and detailed documentation. Compliance requires meticulous attention to every aspect of operations, from the initial assessment and care planning process to infection control, medication management, and emergency preparedness. Licenses are subject to regular surveys and renewal; they typically require renewal every 1-2 years, contingent upon successful annual inspections and adherence to all state and federal standards.

Understanding these rules is not just about passing an inspection; it’s about creating a safe, effective, and high-quality environment for your residents. The DCH and CMS provide extensive resources, but the complexity can be daunting.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Not all nursing facilities are the same. Georgia’s market supports multiple Nursing Facility models, each with different clinical, staffing, and financial considerations. While all operate under the same core license, specialization can be a key differentiator and a driver of profitability. Common program variants include:

  • Traditional Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs): These facilities provide long-term 24-hour medical oversight and personal care for residents who are medically stable but require ongoing nursing support.
  • Post-Acute Rehabilitation Units: Often co-located within a larger SNF, these units focus on short-term, intensive physical, occupational, and speech therapy for patients recovering from surgery, stroke, or serious illness. They are a key link between hospitals and a return to home.
  • Specialized Memory Care Units: These are secure, dedicated wings or floors designed for residents with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. They require specialized staff training, higher staffing ratios (e.g., 1:12 in Georgia), and environmental modifications to ensure resident safety and quality of life.
  • Dual-Eligible Focused Facilities: These facilities specialize in caring for residents who are eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid. They require sophisticated billing and case management capabilities to navigate the complexities of both payment systems.

Program size typically ranges from smaller 30-bed facilities in rural areas to large 150+ bed centers in urban markets. Market analysis is crucial. Demand is strongest in metropolitan Atlanta and its surrounding suburbs, where occupancy rates are high but competition is also fierce. In contrast, many rural regions have limited availability and may offer entry opportunities with less competition, though workforce recruitment can be a challenge. Your choice of specialization and location will fundamentally shape your business model, staffing needs, and referral strategy.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can apply for a license, you must establish a formal business entity. In Georgia, providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp). Each has different implications for liability, taxation, and administration. Consulting with a legal and financial advisor is essential to choose the right structure for your goals.

Once your entity is formed, you must complete several key administrative steps:

  • Register your business with the Georgia Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Georgia DCH HFRD. This application is extensive and requires detailed information about your ownership, organizational structure, key personnel, financial viability, and the physical facility.

Licensing timelines in Georgia are significant. From initial planning to receiving approval to operate, the process generally ranges from 12 to 18 months. This timeline can be affected by the completeness of your application, the time required for facility construction or renovation, and the DCH’s schedule for conducting its initial architectural review and on-site licensure survey.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to success and is essential for securing financing. It must include realistic financial projections based on Georgia’s specific market conditions.

Startup costs for a nursing facility are substantial. While highly variable, they can range from $500,000 for leasing and equipping a smaller, existing facility to well over $10 million for new construction. These costs include property acquisition, construction/renovation, architectural fees, furniture, fixtures, medical equipment, and initial licensing fees.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by labor. Staffing represents approximately 50-60% of total operating costs in a typical nursing facility. Other major expenses include mortgage/lease payments, utilities, food, medical supplies, insurance, and administrative overhead.

Your revenue model will be based on a mix of payers. Typical reimbursement and revenue ranges in Georgia include:

  • Medicaid: The primary payer for long-term care residents, with FY 2024-2025 per diem rates ranging from $589.62 to $707.54. Rates vary based on resident acuity and facility-specific factors.
  • Medicare: Covers short-term, post-acute rehabilitation stays (typically up to 100 days). Medicare rates are generally much higher than Medicaid but are for a limited duration.
  • Private Pay: Residents who pay out-of-pocket. These rates are set by the facility and are typically the highest, often exceeding $300-$400 per day.

With a strong operational plan, providers operating at a target occupancy of 85-90% can generally achieve 5-12% profit margins. A well-run facility can expect to reach its break-even point within 12 to 18 months of opening, assuming a successful ramp-up in census.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

The physical environment is a core component of your license and your ability to provide safe care. Whether you build new or renovate an existing building, the facility must meet stringent state and federal codes.

Key facility requirements for a Georgia nursing facility include:

  • Compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) for accessibility.
  • Adherence to the Life Safety Code (LSC), which governs fire safety, building construction, and emergency egress.
  • Private or semi-private resident rooms that meet specific square footage requirements per resident.
  • A commercial-grade kitchen and dining areas that meet public health standards.
  • Dedicated areas for therapy services, resident activities, and administrative functions.
  • Strategically located nurse’s stations with secure medication storage and preparation areas.
  • Emergency power generators and reliable resident call systems.

Location selection is a strategic decision that should consider zoning regulations, accessibility for families and emergency vehicles, proximity to hospital referral partners, and the availability of a qualified local workforce. The DCH HFRD must approve all architectural plans before construction or renovation begins, and the finished building must pass a final inspection before a license is issued.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is your most valuable asset and the key to providing quality care. Georgia has specific requirements for key positions and overall staffing levels. Required roles in a nursing facility typically include:

  • Licensed Nursing Home Administrator: The facility’s leader must hold a Georgia Nursing Home Administrator License and have at least two years of relevant experience.
  • Director of Nursing (DON): A Registered Nurse (RN) responsible for overseeing all clinical services and nursing staff.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Provide skilled nursing care, assessments, and supervision.
  • Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs): Administer medications and provide direct nursing care under the supervision of an RN.
  • Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs): Provide the majority of hands-on personal care and assistance with daily living. Georgia requires CNAs to meet specific staff-to-resident ratios (e.g., 1:15 on waking shifts, 1:20 on non-waking shifts, and 1:12 in memory care units).
  • Support Staff: Including an Activities Director, Social Worker, Registered Dietitian, and housekeeping/maintenance personnel.

Training is a major focus of regulatory oversight. In Georgia, Certified Nursing Assistants must complete 75 hours of initial state-approved training and pass a competency exam. All CNAs must also complete 12 hours of annual continuing education. All licensed staff must maintain their state licenses in good standing. Furthermore, all employees must receive ongoing training in critical areas like resident rights, infection control, abuse and neglect prevention, HIPAA, and emergency procedures.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Operational excellence and regulatory compliance are built on a foundation of comprehensive, well-written policies and procedures. Georgia’s DCH requires every nursing facility to develop and maintain a detailed policy manual that governs all aspects of its operation. This manual is a living document that must be reviewed and updated regularly.

Georgia requires written policies covering areas such as:

  • Resident Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Policies
  • Comprehensive Resident Assessment and Care Planning
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI)
  • Infection Prevention and Control Program
  • Medication Management and Administration
  • Staffing Plans and Personnel Policies
  • Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
  • Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting

Central to your operations is the Individualized Care Plan. Following a comprehensive assessment, a unique care plan must be developed for each resident, outlining their specific needs, goals, and preferences. This plan must be developed by an interdisciplinary team, including the resident and their family, and must be reviewed and updated at least quarterly or whenever there is a significant change in the resident’s condition.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many businesses, marketing a nursing facility is less about direct-to-consumer advertising and more about building strong, trust-based relationships with professional referral sources. Your census will be built on your reputation for quality, compliance, and responsiveness.

Referrals for nursing facilities in Georgia typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Physician practices and specialty clinics
  • Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) that manage Medicaid and Medicare Advantage members
  • Social workers and community-based senior services, such as Area Agencies on Aging
  • Home health and hospice agencies
  • Other long-term care providers, such as assisted living facilities

Successful providers focus on being a reliable partner to these referrers. This means ensuring a smooth and timely admission process, providing excellent clinical communication, and demonstrating superior patient outcomes through data. Your compliance record, star rating on CMS’s Care Compare website, and survey history are your most powerful marketing tools.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of the regulatory journey. Your facility will be subject to ongoing oversight from both state and federal agencies.

Oversight includes unannounced annual surveys conducted by the Georgia DCH HFRD on behalf of both the state and CMS. These inspections are comprehensive, covering everything from resident care and clinical records to kitchen sanitation and building maintenance. Inspectors will interview residents and staff, observe care delivery, and meticulously review your documentation.

Inspections are focused on identifying deficiencies. Common deficiencies cited in nursing facilities often relate to:

  • Infection control lapses (e.g., improper hand hygiene, equipment sanitation)
  • Accident prevention and supervision
  • Food safety and sanitation
  • Inaccurate or incomplete care planning and assessments
  • Medication administration errors or improper storage
  • Failure to protect resident dignity and rights

Maintaining a state of continuous readiness is essential. This involves implementing a robust Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program to proactively identify and correct issues. Keeping your policies, procedures, and all resident and staff records audit-ready at all times is not just a best practice—it’s a requirement for survival.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Nursing Facility in Georgia?

  • The entire process, from business planning and financing to construction, licensing, and opening your doors, typically takes 12 to 18 months. This timeline can vary significantly based on whether you are building a new facility or acquiring an existing one, the completeness of your application, and DCH inspection schedules.

What licenses are required?

  • The primary license is a Nursing Facility license issued by the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD). Additionally, the facility’s chief executive must hold a valid Georgia Nursing Home Administrator License.

What reimbursement is available?

  • Reimbursement comes from a mix of sources. The largest is Georgia Medicaid, with FY 2024-2025 per diem rates for long-term care ranging from $589.62 to $707.54. Medicare provides higher reimbursement for short-term, post-acute rehabilitation stays. Private pay residents and some long-term care insurance policies are also significant revenue sources.

Conclusion

Starting a Nursing Facility in Georgia is a complex but rewarding venture. The state’s growing demand, coupled with strong reimbursement rates, creates a favorable environment for entrepreneurs dedicated to providing high-quality care. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, develop a highly-trained and compassionate staff, and build strong relationships with hospital and community referral partners are positioned for long-term success and a meaningful impact on the lives of their residents.
